subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage:
Thursday, night.
Day four since the mistake. I sent the client report with last month's figures in it. Everyone says it was easy to fix. I can't stop replaying it: my hand on the mouse, the wrong file, the send button.
Today it got worse. I checked one email six times before sending. I sent an invoice late because I kept second-guessing the amount. Then I made a new typo, in a place I never make typos.
Jasleen stopped by my desk. "You look wrecked. Want lunch tomorrow? Or a word with the lead?" I said, "Maybe tomorrow." That's what I always say.
The mistake was one afternoon. This part is what is actually costing me.
— Deepak

qa.q: How many times did Deepak check one email before sending it?
What was Deepak feeling while replaying the mistake?
qa.a: Deepak was ashamed and anxious, unable to stop replaying it and doubting every task.

qa.q: What could Deepak do about the spiral of self-blame?
qa.a: Deepak could accept Jasleen's offer of lunch or talk to the lead, and treat the mistake as a fixed event with a fix.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt seeing Deepak's state at the desk?
qa.a: Jasleen was concerned and kind, offering lunch and a word with the lead.

grounding: The diary shows an employee replaying an error for days and doubting every task, becoming slower and more error-prone, so that shame harms work as much as carelessness.

passage:
Vikas: you ok? you missed cricket again
Jagdish: can't. rechecking the reports
Vikas: the mistake was 2 weeks ago yaar
Jagdish: I know. I keep replaying it. if I missed one decimal, what else did I miss
Vikas: did your manager say anything?
Jagdish: she said it's fixed. move on
Jagdish: but I've checked today's file 6 times. still not sent
Vikas: 6??
Jagdish: and yesterday I sent the wrong version because I was so tired from checking
Vikas: that's the 2nd mistake FROM worrying about the 1st
Jagdish: I know. I feel useless 😞
Vikas: you're not useless. you're exhausted. talk to your manager about it tomorrow? and come for chai tonight
Jagdish: ok. chai.

qa.q: How many times has Jagdish checked today's file?
qa.a: 6 times, and it's still not sent.
Jagdish feels useless and anxious, stuck replaying the old mistake.

qa.q: What could help Jagdish break the cycle?
qa.a: Talking to the manager about the worry, agreeing one clear check to do once, and resting, as Vikas suggests, instead of rechecking endlessly.

qa.q: How does Jagdish's spiral look to Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas sees a friend exhausted and making new errors from worry, and cares enough to push for a break over chai.

grounding: It shows an employee replaying an error and rechecking everything, becoming slower and making a new mistake, showing how shame can hurt performance.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage:
At the sugar factory's office outside Kolhapur, Varun had entered a farmer's cane payment wrongly three weeks ago. It was caught and corrected within a day. The farmer got his money.
Varun didn't let it go. Every evening on the bus home he replayed the number in his head. At work he checked each entry four, five times, and the daily register, which used to take him two hours, now took five. On Monday he forgot to send the transport bills at all, because he was rechecking last week's.
Pradeep, the senior clerk who had worked there twenty years, finally stopped at his desk. 'Varun, your old mistake cost one day. This fear is costing you a week, every week.' Varun stared at the register. He hadn't thought of it that way.

qa.q: How long did the daily register take Varun now?
qa.a: Five hours, when it used to take him two.

qa.q: What is Varun feeling on the bus rides home?
qa.a: He is anxious and ashamed, replaying the wrong number again and again long after it was fixed.

qa.q: What else could help Varun check well without spiralling?
qa.a: He could agree with Pradeep on one set check for each entry, and talk openly about the fear instead of hiding it behind extra checks.

qa.q: How does Varun's spiral look to Pradeep?
qa.a: Pradeep sees a capable clerk losing a week each week to fear, and is concerned enough to say so plainly.

grounding: It shows an employee replaying a small error and rechecking everything, becoming slower and missing work, as shame damages performance.
